The question I put to the Minister of Labour involves none of the normal partisan antagonism associated with questions asked on the orders of the day. But I am concerned by the fact that throughout Ontario the company I mentioned, the Federal Life and Casualty Company of 191 Eglinton avenue east, Toronto, Ontario, is circulating a business reply card which says:
Just fill in the particulars and drop in the nearest mail box for free information on the federal social security plan.
The main message, on the other side of the card, begins with a bit of "jingles". It says:
Free information. Do not delay. Fill out and mail today. Important! If you have received your social

maintopic: SOCIAL INSURANCE-DISTRIBUTION OF BUSINESS CARDS BY TORONTO INSURANCE COMPANY
speechtext: The real crux of this deception is the insertion of the words "If you have received your social insurance number". What relation there can be between the social insurance numbers which were touted so thoroughly by the Department of Labour and what appears to be a private plan is beyond me, but obviously an unwary person getting such a card as this is almost certain to assume that if he replies he will receive some information with regard to a federal security plan which exists. Mr. Speaker, you will recall that earlier in the day I raised a question in regard to turkey producers. I placed my question before the minister in this way: "Realizing that the minister has had recent consultations with the Canadian turkey producers in regard to their request for an embargo or curtailment of imports, would the minister say what his advice was to these people at that time?" I went on to say that this has been a contentious question and is of course very important to the


turkey producers across the country. I was also prompted to raise the question because it had been raised on September 22 this year, as is recorded at page 8332 of Hansard, by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp), at which time there was no reply from the parliamentary secretary. I believe the minister would have answered the question today had Mr. Speaker allowed him to proceed. It may be the minister has not yet seen fit to meet these people, but I understand he did meet them.
It is my understanding that the importation of turkeys into Canada up to the end of August amounted to something in the neighbourhood of eight million pounds, whereas prior to this time, under the protection afforded by the previous administration I believe the total amount allowed into the country was four million pounds in one year. It is also my understanding that cold storage plants and the like are filled with turkeys and other fowl now, ready for the traditional Thanksgiving market, and the same situation will naturally prevail not too many months hence. It was also brought to my attention upon inquiry that the price of turkeys has dropped something like a cent and a half or two cents a pound since these imports have been allowed into Canada. This is a downward trend. I would imagine this would obviously result in a downward trend in other categories of fowl in this particular market for Canadian producers.
It seems to me I recall that about one year ago the chain stores had a method of using these particular birds as loss leaders, and the pressure of competition certainly made the purchase of such birds at this time of year very easy for the housewife. The producers are very concerned that the area covered by the embargo protection was lifted by the government, after it took many years prior to the change of government in 1957 to convince the government that such was necessary. But in 1957 the producers did succeed in this and we are now asking what advice the minister gave these people when he met them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation as far as turkeys are concerned is this. I attended the annual meeting of the producers in Winnipeg and spoke to the executive there, and we went into the situation very carefully. I believe the original quota was put on in 1958. Eviscerated turkeys were coming in from the United States at a time when we did not have the know-how as far as evisceration

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
was concerned. A quota was established of four million pounds. In addition to that there is now a duty of 5 cents a pound with cents a pound for the discounted dollar and 1 cent for freight. It is true that something over seven to eight million pounds of turkeys have been imported into Canada in the last few weeks, but this has dried up, as we hoped it would, as the turkey market in the United States firmed up.
These imports are tied in with a very wide policy of exports to the United States. At the same time as these imported turkeys came into Canada, 30,000 head of cattle were imported into Canada due to lower prices in the United States. They were able to move this way with all of their other meat products. There is about 20 to 25 per cent protection so far as turkeys are concerned and 5 to 6 per cent protection so far as other meat products are concerned.
It was the feeling of the government of Canada that with this protection the situation was still not serious enough to call for quotas because we had to consider the general agreement on tariffs and trade and make sure we committed no contravention as far as agriculture in Canada is concerned. In discussing this question with the turkey people, they informed me they would send me the resolutions passed at their annual meeting and would submit what they thought we should do about the situation. I have received only one communication so far, although I have written to them again and suggested that their requests should also be backed up by the farm unions and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, with whom they could have a frank discussion in connection with meat imports into Canada. They have not yet indicated whether they will be able to do so; nevertheless they did suggest that if we were able to impose a tariff consistent with value for duty at 3$ cents a pound on live turkeys they would be able to live with the eviscerated turkeys which came into Canada.
That is the situation at the moment. I am still waiting to hear from them but I can assure the hon. member that the government will be pleased to consider any further suggestions they have to offer.
